papers.title: TMEM55B downregulation promotes neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease models.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Lysosomal distribution is critical for numerous biological functions within the cell, including protein degradation in autophagosomes, cholesterol homeostasis, and cell invasion. Changes in the positioning of lysosomes and dysregulation of lysosomal trafficking are known to contribute to different human pathologies, such as lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Here we report the critical role of the lysosomal T ransmembrane P rotein 55B (TMEM55B) in mediating neurodegeneration. Using human clinical-pathological datasets, transgenic flies and iPSC-derived neurons, we demonstrate that loss of function of dTMEM55 potentiates neuronal degeneration. We found that TMEM55B levels are lowered in severe Alzheimer's Disease (AD) cases, validated from microarray, single neuron and total RNA Seq datasets from brain sections of the ROSMAP cohort. Our results demonstrates that loss of function of dTMEM55 results in accumulation of lysosomes in the fly's larval neuronal axons, enhances Tau-mediated retinal degeneration, locomotory dysfunction, lethality, and cell death in the fly AD model. The iPSC-derived AD neurons exhibit reduced TMEM55B levels, autophagic flux defects and increased accumulation of phosphorylated Tau in the lysosomes, confirming the observations in the fly. Overall, our findings indicate that TMEM55B downregulation could contribute to neurodegeneration through defects in lysosomal transport, potentially hindering autophagic clearance of Tau. Our findings have significant relevance in validating the role of lysosomal proteins in normal lysosomal function and maintaining healthy neurons. This work supports continued research into lysosome-mediated neurodegeneration and may provide a basis for exploring potential therapeutic approaches for lysosome-associated neuronal disorders. HIGHLIGHTS: TMEM55B expression is significantly reduced in postmortem brain tissues of patients with severe AD. Genetic loss of TMEM55B enhances Tau-mediated neurodegeneration in Drosophila , indicating a conserved neuroprotective function. TMEM55B regulates neuronal lysosomal positioning across species, and its loss disrupts lysosomal transport.iPSC-derived Alzheimer's disease neurons exhibit late-stage TMEM55B downregulation concomitant with increased accumulation of pathological phosphorylated Tau.Impaired lysosomal trafficking provides a mechanistic link between TMEM55B loss and progressive neurodegeneration.

papers.title: JIP4 deficiency causes a lysosomal storage disease arising from impaired cystine efflux.
papers.abstract: Lysosomes break down macromolecules, clear cellular waste and recycle nutrients such as cystine. We describe a novel mechanism whereby JIP4 regulates lysosomal cystine storage by controlling the abundance of cystinosin (CTNS), the transporter responsible for lysosomal cystine efflux. To this end, JIP4, previously characterized as a motor adaptor and kinase signaling scaffold, suppresses TMEM55B-dependent ubiquitylation of CTNS. Loss of JIP4 reduces CTNS protein levels, leading to lysosomal cystine accumulation and lysosomal storage defects that phenocopy loss of CTNS in both human cells and the renal proximal tubules of JIP4 knockout mice. These phenotypes mirror cystinosis, the lysosomal storage disease caused by CTNS loss-of-function. Our findings thus reveal a fundamental process that controls the efflux of lysosomal cystine and has relevance to understanding human disease arising from JIP4 mutations.

papers.title: Revealing the transcriptomic organization of extrasomatic interfaces using SCOUBI
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) generates substantial transcript signal outside segmented cell bodies, which is generally discarded by analysis tools. This is especially problematic for brain ST data, as neuronal mRNAs can be localized far from somata – in axons, dendrites, and synaptic compartments – and up to half of the transcripts in ST data may lie outside cell bodies. Here, we present SCOUBI, a computational framework that identifies axon-dendrite interfaces from extrasomatic RNA in ST data, revealing a hitherto overlooked layer of molecular function in neural tissues. It first partitions extrasomatic space into axon- and dendrite-enriched compartments based on known marker genes, using a neural network trained to maximize marker specificity and inter-compartment communication signals. It then defines interfaces as loci where predicted axonal and dendritic compartments converge and exhibit ligand–receptor colocalization. Applied to mouse brain, SCOUBI creates maps of axonal and dendritic compartments and their interfaces that align with known spatial patterns of neurite and synaptic distribution. It identifies transcriptomic differences between interfaces and the surrounding extrasomatic space, revealing region-specific signatures of neuronal signaling and synaptic plasticity. By comparing interface transcript enrichment with local somatic expression, SCOUBI identifies genes that preferentially localize at sites of intercellular communication rather than simply reflecting nearby cell bodies. SCOUBI reveals interface-associated transcripts beyond established synaptic genes, with molecular signatures reproducible across independent samples and imaging platforms. In summary, SCOUBI transforms a substantial and often-discarded aspect of ST data into an interpretable readout of subcellular organization and neural signaling.

papers.title: Peptide-centric proteomics reveals molecular subtypes of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex, age-related disease that continues to increase in incidence worldwide. Although some cases are caused by known pathogenic mutations, the majority of cases are sporadic, with uncertain etiology and commonly complicated by comorbid diseases. To better understand the molecular landscape of AD we constructed a unique brain sample set free from neuropathologic comorbidities. This cohort consists of autosomal dominant AD dementia, sporadic AD dementia, cognitively normal individuals with high AD neuropathologic change - a condition called resilient to AD, and cognitively normal cases with no or minimal AD neuropathologic change. Through quantitative mass spectrometry proteomics we obtain measures of peptides mapping to A-beta; and to tau, capturing differences in the histopathologic burden of disease. Correlations of these peptide abundance differences within sporadic AD dementia cases in the superior and medial temporal gyrus indicate the presence of two separate sporadic AD phenotypes. Additional differences are characterized at a peptide level between sporadic AD dementia and autosomal dominant AD dementia in the inferior parietal lobe and caudate nucleus. These findings indicate both shared and distinct molecular features in AD influenced by cause and age of onset of disease.

papers.title: Engineering iPSC-Derived Organoids for Disease Modeling and Regenerative Medicine: Differentiation Strategies, Functional Maturation, and Translational Challenges
papers.abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived organoids are three-dimensional in vitro models that recapitulate se-lected structural and functional features of human tissues. They provide useful platforms for studying development and disease, screening drugs, and exploring regenerative medicine. This review examines strategies for generating iPSC-derived organoids across multiple organ systems, with a comparative focus on how differentiation logic and culture design influence organoid development. Specifically, we discuss guided differentiation using developmental signaling cues and unguided approaches that rely on the cells’ intrinsic capacity for self-organization. We also con-sider scaffold-based and scaffold-free culture methods and how these approaches, together with organ-specific proto-cols, affect organoid formation and maturation. In addition, we summarize signaling pathways commonly used to direct differentiation and the biomedical applications of iPSC-derived organoids. Despite their promise, these models may show variability between cell lines, incomplete maturation, and limited oxygen and nutrient delivery to their inner regions, which can contribute to necrotic core formation. Further refinement of differentiation protocols, culture conditions, and characterization standards may improve the reproducibility and physiological relevance of organoids. By comparing differentiation strategies and culture approaches across organ systems, this review provides a framework for understanding how protocol choices shape organoid development and for guiding future studies in disease modeling, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine.

papers.title: SNX13 and SNX14 interorganelle tethers suppress lysosome membrane damage and neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Lysosome membrane permeabilization (LMP) is an emerging signature of neurodegenerative diseases, yet the mechanisms that enable an effective repair are largely undefined, particularly in neurons. Here, we reveal sorting nexin (SNX) proteins SNX13 and SNX14 maintain lysosome membrane lipid composition to support efficient LMP repair and neuronal survival. We identify loss of function mutations in SNX13 in children manifesting a previously unrecognized cerebellar neurodegenerative disorder. Consistently, Snx13 ablation in mice causes cerebellar Purkinje cell death and signatures of ataxia-like motor deficits. We show loss of SNX13 or its ataxia-linked paralog SNX14 perturbs lysosome morphology, positioning, and acidity and causes increased susceptibility to lysosome damage. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation and proteomics, we comprehensively map lysosome proteome remodeling during membrane damage and repair, finding that SNX13 or SNX14 deficiency blunts recruitment of repair machinery, including ESCRTs and PITT pathway proteins, to damaged lysosomes. Mechanistically, we determine SNX13 and SNX14 support lysosome integrity through interorganelle lipid crosstalk. We define SNX13 and SNX14 as lipid binding proteins that localize to ER-lysosome junctions, where they support lysosomal phosphoinositide levels in response to membrane damage. In line with this, loss of SNX13 or SNX14 impairs lysosome PtdIns4P signaling. Altogether, our work reveals a conserved mechanism of interorganelle lipid crosstalk by SNX13/14 family proteins that safeguards lysosome membranes, maintaining them competent for repair, and is defective in cerebellar neurodegeneration.

papers.title: N-terminal mutations R5L and R5H share a common mechanism in disrupting tau condensates on microtubule surfaces
papers.abstract: Tau, an intrinsically disordered protein abundant in neuronal axons, forms cooperative condensates on microtubule (MT) surfaces that regulate motor proteins and protect MTs from severing enzymes. Disease-associated mutations at residue 5 in the N-terminal projection domain of tau, far from the MT-tau binding interface, have been linked to progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) (R5L) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (R5H). While R5L was previously shown to disrupt tau condensate formation on MT surfaces, it remained unclear whether R5H shares this phenotype. Using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that both mutations reduce condensate packing density compared to WT tau under sub-saturating conditions at physiological pH (7.4), indicating impaired tau-tau cooperativity despite their distal location from the MT-tau binding interface. Single-molecule measurements further show both the dwell time and landing rate of tau within condensates are reduced while behavior on bare MTs remains unchanged, implicating weakened tau-tau cooperativity rather than disrupted binding to MTs. Strikingly, mutational analysis identifies the positive charge at residue 5 as critical for tau condensate formation: the charge-preserving R5K substitution retains WT-like behavior, whereas the charge-eliminating R5I substitution behaves like R5H/R5L. Further supporting this mechanism, R5H exhibits a pronounced pH dependence, transitioning from WT-like behavior at pH 6.4 to R5L-like behavior at pH 7.4 upon histidine deprotonation. Together, these findings establish that the positive charge at R5 is critical for tau condensate formation on MT surfaces and identify a common mechanism linking PSP and FTD.

papers.title: Plasma proteomics reveals signatures of cognitive aging and response to the FINGER multidomain lifestyle intervention
papers.abstract: The FINGER trial demonstrated that a multidomain lifestyle intervention benefits cognition in older adults at-risk of dementia, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We measured neurodegeneration-related proteins using the NULISAseq CNS disease panel in 1158 FINGER participants to investigate associations between circulating proteins, cognitive trajectories, and intervention response. Independent of the intervention, ten proteins spanning immune, neuronal, and metabolic processes were associated with poorer cognitive trajectories, with TREM2 among the strongest signals. The intervention led to changes in eight proteins, including CRH, IL-7 and MME. Eleven proteins modified the cognitive response to intervention, with KDR and CRH showing the strongest effect. Complementary Elastic Net analyses confirmed CRH, and further identified PTN and CCL2 as markers of intervention responsiveness. Additional proteins showed APOE ε4- and sex-specific associations with the intervention response. Together, these findings identify proteomic signatures of cognitive response that could inform precision dementia prevention.
